planting.note: Set divisions or nursery pots in spring once soil has warmed, siting crowns slightly above grade in a humus-rich shaded bed.

directions: This Japanese and Korean woodland species produces upright, leathery, dark green fronds from a slow-building crown and stays semi-evergreen through mild winters, dropping fronds only after hard freezes. Grow it in consistently moist, well-drained soil enriched with leaf mold, in part to full shade where summer heat is tempered. It resents soggy winter conditions more than dry spells once established, so improve drainage on heavy clay before planting. Divide congested clumps in early spring, keeping several fronds and a section of rhizome with each division.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in a cool, humus-rich woodland bed; this smaller species suits the front of a shaded border or a rock garden niche.

directions: Native to montane woodlands of Japan and Korea, this compact wood fern is named for the dense covering of pale brown scales along its stipes and rachises, which contrast nicely with the finely cut, deciduous to semi-evergreen fronds. It prefers a cool root zone and steady moisture, doing best where summer heat is moderated by tree canopy or a north-facing slope. Unlike larger Dryopteris relatives it stays tidy and non-spreading, making it useful for smaller shade plantings. Lift and divide only when clumps become crowded, since it resents frequent disturbance.
sources: Flora of Japan (National Museum of Nature and Science, Tokyo)

planting.note: Plant in spring after frost danger passes, siting in a sheltered shaded bed where winters stay mild; in colder zones grow in a container that can be overwintered.

directions: This East Asian and Himalayan species is grown chiefly for its blackish, glossy stipes that carry dark scales and give the whole plant a striking two-tone look against the leathery, deep green fronds. Give it rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in shade with protection from drying winds, since the semi-evergreen fronds can scorch in exposed sites. It is less cold-hardy than many Dryopteris relatives, so mulch the crown heavily where winters dip below the mid-teens Fahrenheit. Divide established clumps in early spring, keeping a healthy portion of rhizome with each piece.

planting.note: Set out divisions or pot-grown plants in spring in a shaded woodland bed; this small evergreen fern also works well along path edges or in a rock garden.

directions: Found from Japan and Korea to Taiwan and parts of the Himalayas, this diminutive evergreen fern forms neat rosettes of glossy, leathery, dark green fronds that hold their color through winter in milder zones. Some fronds produce small plantlets near the tip that can root where they touch soil, giving an easy, low-key way to increase a planting over time. Grow it in humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade with consistent moisture, avoiding waterlogged winter conditions. It stays small and non-aggressive, making it a good choice for tucking among rocks or along a shaded walkway.
sources: Flora of Japan (National Museum of Nature and Science, Tokyo)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in a spacious shaded bed, allowing enough room for the large, arching fronds to spread without crowding neighboring plants.

directions: A larger Japanese relative of the familiar tassel fern, this species produces broad, glossy, dark green fronds emerging from stout crowns wrapped in golden-brown fibrous scales, giving strong architectural presence in a shaded border. It performs best in rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil with shelter from harsh winter wind, holding much of its evergreen foliage through the cold season in milder parts of its range. Established clumps are long-lived and slow to spread, so give them room at planting rather than crowding them with smaller perennials. Remove tattered old fronds in early spring before new growth unfurls.
sources: Flora of Japan (National Museum of Nature and Science, Tokyo)

planting.note: Plant in spring in a cool, sheltered shaded bed with reliable moisture; in borderline climates grow in a large container that can be moved under cover for winter.

directions: Native to New Zealand forests and subalpine scrub, this coarse-textured evergreen fern forms a short trunk-like base topped with stiff, dark green, heavily scaled fronds that give it a distinctly rugged look among softer shade ferns. It wants cool, consistently damp, humus-rich soil and struggles in heat or drought, so it is best suited to maritime or cool-summer gardens with reliable shade. Hard frost and prolonged dry spells are its main limiting factors in cultivation outside its native range. Clear away old, browned fronds at the base periodically to keep the crown tidy and encourage fresh growth.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in a sheltered shaded spot with constant moisture; where winters are cold grow it in a pot that can be brought indoors or into a greenhouse.

directions: Widespread across Australia, southern Africa, and New Zealand, this delicate maidenhair carries finely divided, light green pinnae on wiry, nearly black stipes, forming soft, lacy clumps that spread gently by creeping rhizomes. It needs year-round moisture and humidity along with rich, well-drained soil, wilting quickly if it dries out even briefly. Outside its naturally mild range it is best grown as a container or greenhouse plant, or treated as a seasonal shade planting that is lifted before frost. Trim away damaged fronds at the base rather than mid-frond to keep new growth looking clean.
